Last term I was the new boy in 9B, and I learnt fast who owned the back bench by the window. Mahima, Sharmila and three others shared tiffins, notes and inside jokes. When Sharmila forgot the group chart, Mahima said, "She had a family function, poor thing," and they redid it together at lunch.
Two weeks later I was the one who forgot my part of the science model. Mahima rolled her eyes. "Typical. Some people just don't care." Sharmila told Sir I was "never serious." Nobody asked why. My grandfather had been in hospital that week.
I'm Kunal, and I still remember how hot my ears felt, standing there, knowing the same mistake had two different prices depending on which bench you sat on.

qa.q: What did Kunal forget two weeks after Sharmila forgot the group chart?
qa.a: Kunal forgot his part of the science model.

qa.q: Why did Kunal's ears feel hot as he stood there?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and angry: Sharmila's lapse was excused with sympathy, while his identical one was called not caring, and nobody asked his reason.

qa.q: When the group turned on Kunal in front of Sir, what choice could he have made in that moment?
qa.a: He could calmly tell Sir that his grandfather had been in hospital that week, so his side is heard instead of only the group's verdict.

qa.q: How might Sharmila see her own forgotten chart differently from Kunal's forgotten model?
qa.a: To Sharmila, her lapse had a good reason because her friends explained it for her; Kunal's looks like carelessness because no one in the group knows or asks about his week.

grounding: A teenage boy outside a back-bench group sees them excuse one member's lapse while condemning his identical one.

Class 10C, note after the Thursday inter-house match.
Pranav came off the field quietly today. During the match, Ishita's friends laughed off two missed passes by Dev, one of their own: "Pitch is bumpy." When Pranav slipped and lost the ball, the same group shouted that he was "useless" and "shouldn't even be on the team." I saw him stare at the ground and walk to the far end of the bench, away from everyone. On the walk back, Ishita said he had "ruined it for all of us."
Afterwards I sat with Pranav. He said, "When they miss, it's the pitch. When I miss, it's me." I told him I had seen both moments and that it was not a fair way to judge anyone. Tomorrow I will talk to the whole team about one rule for everyone on the field.
— Ms Rao, class teacher

qa.q: What did the group say when Dev missed two passes?
qa.a: They laughed it off and said, "Pitch is bumpy."

qa.q: What does Pranav's walk to the far end of the bench suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: It suggests he felt hurt and shut out, sure the group would never judge him as kindly as they judged Dev. 😔

qa.q: What choice did Ms Rao make after the match, and why does it matter?
qa.a: Ms Rao chose to sit with Pranav and tell him both moments were seen, so he knew the double standard was real and not in his head.

qa.q: If you were Dev, how might it feel to watch Pranav blamed for a smaller mistake than yours?
qa.a: Dev might feel uneasy or guilty, realising the group covered for the two missed passes and aimed all the anger at Pranav instead.

grounding: A teacher records how a clique excuses its own player's misses but harshly blames Pranav, the boy outside it.

By her third month at the university in Nairobi, Vera had started keeping a quiet tally. The campus café hired students for evening shifts, and the manager, a cheerful man from Nyeri, always seemed to have "just filled" the slots, usually with students who had grown up near Nyeri too. Her flatmate Wanjiru had applied twice, with more free hours than anyone. Both times she got a polite no.
In the lab it was similar: the senior student helped the two from his old school first, then looked round for the rest.
One evening Vera said it plainly. "Wanjiru, I don't think it's you. I think it's where people come from."
Wanjiru was quiet, then nodded slowly. "I thought I was imagining it."
Next morning they listed the dates she had applied and asked the student welfare office how café shifts were meant to be given out.

qa.q: How many times had Wanjiru applied for the café shifts?
qa.a: Wanjiru had applied twice.

qa.q: What does Wanjiru mean by 'I thought I was imagining it'?
qa.a: She had sensed something unfair but doubted herself, so hearing Vera name the pattern made her feel less alone and less to blame.

qa.q: What choice did Vera and Wanjiru make the next morning, and why was it a useful turning point?
qa.a: They listed the dates and asked the welfare office how shifts should be given, turning a vague hunch into something that could be checked fairly.

qa.q: How might the café manager see his own hiring if the pattern were pointed out?
qa.a: He may honestly feel he just trusts people he knows, and only seeing the dates side by side might show him that others never got a real chance.

grounding: A student notices café jobs and lab help flowing to people from one home region and names it to the flatmate left out.

Six weeks into the internship, something is bothering me. My manager went to the same college as me, and I get easy trust: "Tarun's from our place, he'll manage." qa.a: Megha may feel she has to prove herself twice over, and hearing about the lunch late could make her feel quietly outside the team.

passage:
Last spring I sat on my first hiring panel. I'm Uma, the youngest woman on it, and I was nervous about getting it wrong. One candidate, Pankaj, had grown up three streets from my school in Coimbatore. We laughed about the same bakery. I liked him instantly, and that was exactly what worried me.
Before the interviews I had written four things on a card: problem-solving, clarity, teamwork, willingness to learn. After Pankaj left, I scored him against the card, not against the bakery. Then I asked myself: if he had come from a town I'd never heard of, would I give him the same marks? Honestly, one mark lower.
I also asked the team to add two candidates from colleges we never visit. One of them, a quiet woman from Silchar, got the job.

qa.q: What four things did Uma write on her card?
qa.a: Problem-solving, clarity, teamwork and willingness to learn.

qa.q: Why did liking Pankaj instantly worry Uma?
qa.a: She knew the shared bakery and hometown could make her rate him higher than his answers deserved, and she wanted to be fair. 🤔

qa.q: What choice did Uma make after scoring Pankaj, and how did it change the result?
qa.a: She asked whether she'd give the same marks to someone from an unfamiliar town, dropped his score by one, and pushed for candidates from unvisited colleges, one of whom got the job.

qa.q: How might the woman from Silchar see this hiring if Uma hadn't pushed for new colleges?
qa.a: She might never have been interviewed at all, and would likely have assumed the company simply wasn't open to people like her.

grounding: A young woman on a hiring panel uses a criteria card, seeks candidates unlike herself and tests her call against her hometown pull.
